ds_context: The industrial robot is prone to failures in its various components, including the robot arm, gripper, vision system, and control system. The robot arm is susceptible to wear and tear of joints and bearings due to high cyclic load, lack of lubrication, and contamination, leading to malfunctions or complete failure. This failure mode has a high severity and moderate detectability, as it can be detected through regular maintenance and inspection, but may not be noticeable until it becomes severe. The gripper is prone to damage to fingers or failure of gripping mechanism due to overuse, misalignment, or mechanical failure, with high severity and high detectability. The vision system can experience failure of the camera or loss of calibration due to mechanical, electrical, or software failure, with high severity and high detectability. The control system can have failure of control software or hardware due to software bugs, electrical or mechanical failure, with high severity and high detectability. To prevent and predict failures, regular maintenance and inspection of all components, prompt attention to any abnormalities, and timely replacement of worn-out parts are crucial.
question_context: To ensure the reliable performance of industrial robots, it's crucial to monitor key performance indicators (KPIs) such as response time, cycle time, and error rate for anomalies. External factors like temperature and humidity can also impact the robot's performance and should be included in the anomaly model. Typical failure modes include mechanical, electrical, and software failures. The desired performance metrics for the anomaly detection model include low false positive and false negative rates. Leveraging prior work or existing models for anomaly detection in industrial robots can be beneficial. Historical failures should be analyzed to understand their causes and detection methods. Anomaly detection can be improved by identifying specific patterns in sensor data, focusing on critical components, and using accurate and reliable sensors. Regular maintenance and inspections, along with real-time sensor data, can help detect failures early. Setting specific metrics or threshold values for component degradation can also aid in predicting failures. Building an anomaly model can lead to improved outcomes and benefits, such as reduced downtime and increased productivity. The range, frequency, and type of sensor data collected are critical factors in developing an effective anomaly model. Access to historical data or incident reports can help in building a comprehensive model. Specific sensors can detect wear and tear in joints and bearings, while software or algorithms can be used to detect failures in control systems, mechanical components, and vision systems.
